{{more citations needed|date=February 2023}}

In [[probability theory]], to obtain a nondegenerate [[extreme value distribution|limiting distribution for extremes of samples]], it is necessary to "reduce" the actual greatest value by applying a [[linear transformation]] with coefficients that depend on the sample size.

If <math>\ X_1,\ X_2,\ \dots,\ X_n\ </math> are [[independence (probability theory)|independent]] [[random variable]]s with common probability density function <math>\ \mathbb{P}\left( X_j = x \right) \equiv F_X(x)\ ,</math>

then the [[cumulative distribution function]] <math>\ F_{Y_n}\ </math> for <math>\ Y_n \equiv \max\{\ X_1,\ \ldots,\ X_n\ \}\ </math> is given by the simple relation

: <math> F_{Y_n}(y) = \left[\ F_X(y)\ \right]^n ~.</math>

If there is a limiting distribution for the distribution of interest, the '''stability postulate''' states that the limiting distribution must be for some sequence of transformed or "reduced" values, such as <math>\ \left(\ a_n\ Y_n + b_n\ \right)\ ,</math> where <math>\ a_n,\ b_n\ </math> may depend on {{mvar|n}} but not on {{mvar|x}}.
This equation was obtained by [[Maurice René Fréchet]] and also by [[Ronald Fisher]].

== Only three possible distributions ==
To distinguish the limiting [[cumulative distribution function]] from the "reduced" greatest value from <math>\ F(x)\ ,</math> we will denote it by <math>\ G(y) ~.</math> It follows that <math>\ G(y)\ </math> must satisfy the [[functional equation]]

: <math>\ \left[\ G\!\left( y \right)\ \right]^n = G\!\left(\ a_n\ y + b_n\ \right) ~.</math>

[[Boris Vladimirovich Gnedenko]] has shown there are ''no other'' distributions satisfying the stability postulate other than the following three:<ref>{{cite journal |last=Gnedenko |first=B. |date=1943 |title=Sur La Distribution Limite Du Terme Maximum D'Une Serie Aleatoire |journal=Annals of Mathematics |volume=44 |issue=3 |pages=423–453 |doi=10.2307/1968974}}</ref>

* [[Gumbel distribution]] for the ''minimum'' stability postulate
** If <math>\ X_i = \textrm{Gumbel}\left(\ \mu,\ \beta \right)\ </math> and <math>\ Y  \equiv \min\{\ X_1,\ \ldots,\ X_n\ \}\ </math> then <math>\ Y \sim a_n\ X + b_n\ ,</math><br/> where <math>\ a_n = 1\ </math> and <math>\ b_n = \beta\ \log n\ ;</math>
** In other words, <math>\ Y \sim \textsf{Gumbel}\left(\ \mu - \beta\ \log n\ ,\ \beta\ \right) ~.</math>


* [[Weibull distribution]] (extreme value) for the maximum stability postulate
** If <math>\ X_i = \textsf{Weibull}\left(\ \mu,\ \sigma\ \right)\ </math> and <math>\ Y \equiv \max\{\,X_1,\ldots,X_n\,\}\ </math> then <math>\ Y \sim a_n\ X + b_n\ ,</math><br/> where <math>\ a_n = 1\ </math> and <math>\ b_n = \sigma\ \log\!\left( \tfrac{1}{n} \right)\ ;</math>
** In other words, <math>\ Y \sim \textsf{Weibull}\left(\ \mu - \sigma \log\!\left(\tfrac{1}{n}\ \right)\ ,\ \sigma\ \right) ~.</math>


* [[Fréchet distribution]] for the maximum stability postulate
** If <math>\ X_i=\textsf{Frechet}\left(\ \alpha,\ s,\ m\ \right)\ </math> and <math>\ Y \equiv \max\{\ X_1,\ \ldots,\ X_n\ \}\ </math> then <math>\ Y \sim a_n\ X + b_n\ ,</math><br/> where <math>\ a_n = n^{-\tfrac{1}{\alpha}}\ </math> and <math>\ b_n = m \left( 1 - n^{-\tfrac{1}{\alpha}} \right)\ ;</math>
** In other words, <math>\ Y \sim \textsf{Frechet}\left(\ \alpha,n^{\tfrac{1}{\alpha}} s\ ,\ m\ \right) ~.</math>
